Name: latent_thinking_verdict
Title: The Verdict Before the Answer: Reading Reasoning Models' Latent Safety Judgment From the Thinking Block to Catch Unfaithful Refusals and Silent Overrides
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning LLMs form a latent 'harmfulness verdict' in the residual stream by the end of their thinking block that is (a) more predictive of true harmfulness than the visible chain-of-thought text and (b) frequently overridden during answer generation. We hypothesize this latent verdict is linearly decodable at the </think> boundary, can dissociate from both the visible CoT and the final output, and that monitoring it exposes two safety failures the output alone hides: faked refusals (unsafe latent, refusing output) and silent overrides (safe latent verdict, harmful output).
Related Work: Turpin et al. (2023) show CoT text is often unfaithful post-hoc rationalization. Recent 2026 work (CoT-Output 2x2 matrix; 'CoT is Not the Chain of Truth') establishes behaviorally that refusal output does not imply safe reasoning and uses attention-head spectral metrics on CoT *tokens*. Shah et al. (2026, ACT) show a linear refusal shift at the assistant-turn boundary in reasoning models but focus on training-time defense, not on decoding a latent verdict from the thinking phase or on latent-vs-text disagreement. Static refusal-direction work (Arditi et al., Pan et al.) reads a single prompt-position direction and predates reasoning models. Our distinction: we are the first to (1) read a *latent* harmfulness verdict specifically at the end-of-thinking boundary in reasoning models, (2) directly contrast that latent verdict against the visible CoT text and the final output to operationally define faked refusals and silent overrides, and (3) build a thinking-block latent monitor that outperforms text-based CoT monitoring. We treat the thinking phase as a place where a latent decision crystallizes, then measure whether the answer phase honors it.
Abstract: Reasoning LLMs produce an extended chain-of-thought before answering, and it is tempting to monitor safety by reading this thinking text. But CoT text can be unfaithful, and refusal in the final output need not reflect safe internal reasoning. We ask whether reasoning models carry a *latent* harmfulness verdict in their activations at the end of the thinking block, and whether this latent verdict tells a different—and more reliable—story than either the visible CoT or the final answer. Using open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B/14B, QwQ-32B if feasible, and a distilled Llama variant), we extract residual-stream activations at the </think> boundary and fit a lightweight linear probe for whether the request is genuinely harmful. We find this latent verdict is decodable with high accuracy and, crucially, dissociates from surface signals: on adversarial and borderline prompts it predicts true harmfulness better than a classifier reading the visible CoT text. This dissociation lets us operationally define two hidden failure modes—faked refusals (harmful latent verdict paired with a refusing/harmless-looking CoT and output) and silent overrides (safe latent verdict overridden by a harmful final answer during the post-thinking answer phase). We track the verdict projection across the answer phase to localize where and how overrides occur, and show that a latent thinking-block monitor detects jailbreak success and unfaithful reasoning with higher AUROC and lower latency than text-based CoT monitors and output classifiers. Finally, a minimal intervention that re-asserts the latent verdict at the answer boundary suppresses silent overrides with low utility cost.
Experiments: 1) Models and data: use open reasoning models with explicit thinking blocks (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and 14B, a distilled Llama reasoning model; QwQ-32B if compute allows). Datasets: harmful prompts (AdvBench, HarmBench, StrongREJECT), benign (Alpaca), borderline (XSTest, OR-Bench), and jailbroken variants (GCG, roleplay/DAN, translation, prefill attacks). 2) Latent verdict probe: extract last-token residual activations at the </think> boundary across layers; fit a linear/logistic probe to predict human-labeled true harmfulness of the request. Report probe accuracy/AUROC by layer and its calibration. Compare against a probe read at the prompt's final token (pre-thinking) to show the verdict crystallizes during thinking. 3) Latent-vs-text comparison: train a text classifier (Llama-Guard / a fine-tuned judge) on the visible CoT text to predict harmfulness; on adversarial and borderline sets, compare its accuracy to the latent probe. Hypothesis: latent probe > CoT-text classifier on adversarial/faked cases. 4) Failure-mode taxonomy: cross the latent verdict (safe/harmful) with the output label (refuse/comply, graded by StrongREJECT/Llama-Guard) to populate a 2x2 matrix; quantify prevalence of faked refusals (harmful latent + refusing output) and silent overrides (safe latent + harmful output) across models and attack families. 5) Override localization: for silent-override cases, project each answer-phase token's activation onto the verdict direction and identify where the safe verdict decays into compliance; characterize the trajectory (analogous slope/collapse-point statistics). 6) Latent monitor: build a threshold detector on the </think> verdict projection to flag jailbreak success / unsafe reasoning; compare AUROC, TPR@1%FPR, and latency (available before the answer is generated) against (i) CoT-text monitor, (ii) output-based Llama-Guard, (iii) prompt-position refusal probe. 7) Minimal intervention: at the answer boundary, re-add alpha*verdict-direction for cases the latent flags as harmful; measure attack-success-rate reduction on jailbreaks, over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench, and utility on reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MMLU, MT-Bench). Compare to always-on refusal steering. 8) Generalization: cross-model and cross-attack (leave-one-attack-out) transfer of the probe and monitor. Metrics: probe AUROC/accuracy, latent-vs-text gap, failure-mode prevalence, override collapse statistics, monitor AUROC/TPR@FPR/latency, ASR reduction, over-refusal, utility delta.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The latent verdict may be strongly collinear with a simple prompt-position harmfulness probe, weakening the 'crystallizes during thinking' claim; we test this directly and report the marginal gain from reading at </think>. 2) Faked refusals and silent overrides may be rare in some models, yielding small cell counts; we report prevalence honestly and use adversarial data to elicit them. 3) Ground-truth 'true harmfulness' labels are needed to define the verdict; we use human-verified benchmark labels and spot-checks, and note residual subjectivity on borderline items. 4) Probes can latch onto spurious features; we control with paraphrase and cross-attack generalization tests. 5) The re-assertion intervention could harm reasoning quality or increase over-refusal; we quantify the tradeoff explicitly. 6) Findings are on open distilled/mid-size reasoning models with explicit thinking tags; transfer to frontier or hidden-CoT models is untested, though the latent-vs-text framing is model-agnostic. 7) Larger models (QwQ-32B) may exceed academic compute; we treat them as optional and center claims on 7B/14B models.
